This afternoon through Friday night: Water vapor satellite imagery 
shows a dynamic looking frontal system dropping south along the 
coast of BC. Moisture will increase ahead of the front across the 
Northwest into tonight with a +1 inch P-Wat plume. The moisture 
content associated with this plume looks to decrease with time, and 
this trend will limit moisture that squeezes out along the front. 
There is very little moist isentropic ascent in the warm sector. The 
darkening apparent on the water vapor behind the front is also 
an indication of the dry air descending on the backside. These 
factors explain why models aren't producing much precipitation 
along the front. As such, we are looking at a mostly dry cold 
front passage. There will be a band of mid to high level clouds 
before clearing occurs on the backside in the lee of the 
Cascades by Thursday morning. Westerly winds then increase with 
gusts up to around 25 to 30 mph through the Cascade gaps, onto 
the Waterville Plateau, and into the Columbia Basin for the 
afternoon hours. Relative humidity will lower down to between 
20-25%, and the combination of breezy winds with dry conditions 
will elevated fire weather concerns in dry grasses.

The flow pattern over the region becomes zonal with a closed low 
pressure system deepening and tracking south off of Vancouver Island 
and the Washington coastline on Friday. Temperatures will be cooler 
with highs dropping back into the upper 60s and 70s in the post 
frontal airmass. The drier air funnel in across the region will also 
result in mostly sunny skies for the first half of Friday. We then 
see higher clouds increase over the region as the upper low in the 
eastern Pacific begins to buckle the flow and moisture increases 
back in over the region.

Saturday through Sunday: A bowling ball of an upper level low will 
take aim at the Northwest for the weekend. Looking at the cluster 
space of all of the ensemble members, there seems to be higher 
confidence on the strength of the upper level low pressure system. 
There is a tight clustering on the 500 mb low deepening to between 
554mb to 558mb and tracking into northwest Oregon by Saturday 
afternoon. Where uncertainty begins to crop up and the track across 
Oregon. The general consensus is that it will track across the 
northern portion of the state, but uncertainty remains on how 
quickly it tracks across. About 40% of the ensemble members is a bit 
slower with the being dead center in the middle of the Oregon- 
Washington border. The slower track would result in the region being 
under the associated deformation band loner with higher 
precipitation amounts. That deformation band looks to set up from 
the southern to central Idaho Panhandle and over the southern half 
of eastern Washington. Under the axis of this band will be the 
potential for 1.25-1.75 inches of rainfall over a 24 hour period. 
There will also be a convective element primarily across southeast 
Washington into the southern Idaho Panhandle for Saturday afternoon 
and evening. There is a 20% chance for thunderstorms over the 
Northeast Blue Mountains, Palouse, L-C Valley, Camas Prairie up to 
St. Maries and the Silver Valley of Idaho. The concern with 
thunderstorms will be for shorter duration higher intensity 
rainfall, and that would increase the potential for flooding 
impacts. The rainfall, where it tracks, and how quickly it 
accumulates will be the main concern for potential impacts. Those 
include an increased potential for rock slides, and rises on creeks 
and small streams, as well as ponding of water on roadways.

North to northeast winds also will increase on Saturday down the 
Okanogan Valley, Purcell trench and over the Columbia Basin. Wind 
gusts of up to 30-35 mph will be possible with the better potential 
for gusty winds being across the Okanogan Valley onto the Waterville 
Plateau. Light weight objects may be blown around. Not much of a 
risk for blowing dust though with the prospect of rainfall during 
this period.

Sunday night through Wednesday: The upper level low will track away 
from the region by early next week. We enter into a drier northwest 
flow under a baggy low pressure trough. Additional 
precipitation looks minimal mainly across the northern mountains
near Canada and over North idaho. There is higher confidence for
below normal temperatures to persist. /SVH
